title: Jacob
summary: Genesis follows Jacob from the struggle over the family blessing through his flight, years with Laban, return to face Esau, and the growth of his household. At Bethel and again after his night struggle at the Jabbok, the story connects Jacob with the promise given to Abraham; Jacob is later named Israel, linking his family story to the people of Israel.
historical_context: Jacob belongs to the ancestral world of Genesis, where clans, migration, inheritance, and land promise shape the story.
ancient_near_east_context: Genesis places Jacob’s story in households shaped by kinship, marriage, inheritance, work with flocks, and access to land and water. The episodes with Laban and Esau show how household ties and property disputes can shape the family’s future in the narrative. These details describe Genesis’ story world, not a rule that every ancient Near Eastern family lived in the same way.
canonical_context: Jacob’s story explains why Israel is also the name of a people: Genesis identifies Jacob with the name Israel and follows the households of his sons into the next generation. Later biblical passages can therefore speak of Israel as both a person and a people, though each passage’s meaning depends on its own context.
literary_context: The Jacob cycle develops through reversals. Jacob takes the blessing while disguised as Esau, then Laban deceives him over the marriage arrangement; after years away, Jacob returns expecting danger and meets Esau with gifts and an embrace. The story’s repeated turns keep the reader attentive to the gap between Jacob’s plans and the future carried by the promise.
covenantal_significance: The promise given to Abraham is repeated to Jacob at Bethel, where God speaks of land, descendants, and blessing (Genesis 28). After Jacob wrestles through the night, he receives the name Israel and a blessing (Genesis 32). These scenes connect the ancestral promise to Jacob’s descendants, while the family narrative continues to include rivalry, fear, and reconciliation.
canonical_role: Jacob serves as a canonical person anchor, connecting biographical context, key passages, and related places, events, and themes.

interpretive_notes.note: Read the figure as part of a family and promise line, not as an isolated biography.
The family narratives frequently combine faith, failure, and divine promise in the same story.
